prize_parts.citation: For establishing that multivalent biomolecules can demix by liquid-liquid phase separation above a threshold concentration, as a physical-chemical principle for organizing cellular matter without membranes

statement.case_for: I keep B063, but with a narrower claim than in round 1. The discovery I would credit is a principle: multivalent macromolecules demix above a threshold concentration into dense liquid-like phases, and this can organise cytoplasm and nucleus. It rests on quantitative physical chemistry (saturation concentration, valency, interfacial tension, viscoelasticity). It was shown in reconstituted systems with defined components, by Brangwynne and Hyman with P granules in 2009 and by Rosen with multivalent signalling proteins in 2012, and it has been reproduced in very many laboratories. The citation does not need to certify that every reported condensate in vivo is a liquid. It rests on what is demonstrated in vitro and in specific cellular cases. That is the same standard the committee applies when a principle is honoured while its applications are still being mapped. The concept also connects directly to neurodegeneration, where liquid-to-solid transitions of condensates are linked to amyloid formation, which is close to my own work. And it is a prize about the chemistry of living matter, not synthesis or a method, which I think the committee should weigh when it balances fields. Nothing in the round-1 exchange has convinced me that a rival is a stronger case. Several members have convinced me that B063 will not reach five votes this year without a very tight citation.
statement.case_against: The objections raised against me are serious and I do not dismiss them. The in vivo physical state of many condensates is contested, and the link from phase state to function is weaker than the textbook version suggests. Attribution is the other weak point: Pappu's sequence-grammar and theory work and Mittag's work on multivalent interactions are arguably as decisive as Rosen's biochemistry, so a three-name cut is contestable and a five-name credit is impossible under our limit. Somfai also has a point that part of the novelty is the import of established phase-behaviour concepts into cell biology, and a committee could regard the result as Medicine. Finally, no other member configured B063 in round 1, so a majority is not in sight, and I should say that plainly instead of pretending the support count is higher than it is.

responses.point: Linke places condensates third and worries that a prize now would freeze a concept whose boundaries are unsettled, asking whether the discovery separates cleanly from later, broader claims about condensate function.
responses.response: This is the right question, and my answer is to write the citation so that it does. It should name the principle of demixing of multivalent biomolecules into dense phases that organise cellular matter, and say nothing about function in any given condensate or about disease. That claim is supported by the P-granule work and by Rosen's multivalency experiments, and it is not touched by the debate over which in vivo assemblies are equilibrium liquids. I accept that this makes the prize narrower than the field's own rhetoric, and I think it should. I also accept that if the committee will not credit a principle while its in vivo reach is being mapped, B063 fails. On Linke's own B052 I remain unconvinced that this is the better moment, because the PROTAC and glue lineages are separate and the clinical proof is incomplete.

responses.point: Somfai argues that the chemical novelty in B063 is mostly the import of established phase-behaviour concepts into cell biology, that physiological relevance is contested, and that credit across Pappu, Mittag and the wider community makes a three-person citation either vague or wrong.
responses.response: The import point is fair as a description of the history, and I disagree that it counts against the discovery. Flory-Huggins thermodynamics was available for decades, but the demonstration that specific cellular compartments obey it, with measurable thresholds and valency dependence, is the new knowledge, in the way that applying thermodynamics to a new class of matter is chemistry. I agree about attribution and I do not think it can be fully solved: Pappu and Mittag have the strongest claim to the physical-chemical framework, and my choice of Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen privileges the experimental demonstrations over the theory. I would not call that wrong, but I would call it lossy, and I accept that a reader could judge it harder to defend than Hartwig and Buchwald, whose two-person credit is clean. Where I differ is that cleanliness is not by itself the case for B031, given its closeness to the 2010 prize.

responses.point: Zou moved to B055 and says that a phase-separation citation should wait until it is settled which cellular assemblies are truly phase-separated rather than droplet-like only in vitro or on overexpression, preferring a method with direct, repeated validation.
responses.response: I agree that overexpression artefacts are a real problem in this literature, and I would not credit any specific in vivo condensate. The evidence for the principle comes from purified systems with defined stoichiometry and from experiments at endogenous or near-endogenous levels in a smaller number of well-studied cases, and I think that is enough for a principle-level citation. I also disagree that method validation is a better standard than conceptual validation: a method is reproduced because it works, and a principle is reproduced because it explains. Sequencing by synthesis has strong chemistry and is the most mature candidate on the list, but my doubt is whether the committee would be crediting a reversible-terminator reaction or an engineered platform, and the unresolved Rothberg, Ju and Mayer claims leave the two-person cut exposed. I will not rank B055 above B063 unless the committee can say where the decisive chemical step lies.

responses.point: Aili configures B052 (PROTACs and cereblon glues) with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and says that Handa's identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target gives the molecular-glue strand a mechanism, so one citation can cover both lineages.
responses.response: I accept the strength of the principle: event-driven pharmacology through induced proximity is a clear new idea, and I recognise that it has the most opening support. The cereblon result is the better of the two lineages for a mechanism-based citation, since it explains a drug by a molecular target. My problem remains the structure of the credit. A trio of Crews, Deshaies and Handa omits Ciulli, whose rational VHL ligand and ternary-complex structures made the PROTAC principle chemically designable, and it also omits Ito, who worked with Handa on cereblon. A single induced-proximity citation hides that these are two histories. I would not block B052 if the committee agrees a Crews, Deshaies, Handa citation, but I also do not think the missing approved PROTAC drug is a trivial point for a prize whose condition is demonstrated benefit. In practical terms I would move it from seventh to a clear second choice for me, though still not above B063 on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Chabes pairs sequencing by synthesis (Balasubramanian and Klenerman) with base editing (Liu), reading and rewriting DNA as two distinct achievements within three people, and treats the missing Komor, Gaudelli, Nishida and Kondo credit as an accepted cost.
responses.response: The pairing is neat and keeps within the limit of three, but I find that the tidiness comes from the arithmetic. Liu alone for base editing leaves out the two people who did the first cytidine and adenine deaminase experiments, and I would not use a prize to settle priority for the field by omission. I would also not accept two thinly supported parts in place of one strong one; a two-part prize is only attractive when both parts are individually above the bar, and I judge that base editing is not yet there because the clinical record and the Nishida and Kondo parallel work are unresolved. If the committee does want a two-part prize, my own preference would be to pair B063 with something clearly mature rather than with another young candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat liquid-liquid phase separation in cells as chemistry rather than cell biology, which is the question that decides whether B063 is eligible for Chemistry at all.
Whether a citation limited to the in vitro-established principle is accepted as sufficient, or whether the in vivo debate makes any condensate prize premature.
Whether Pappu and Mittag can be left out defensibly when Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen occupy the three places.
Whether I am overweighting a field close to my own: lipid self-assembly and amyloid are near to condensates, and I cannot rule out bias in favour of a physical-chemistry framing.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile, and none requires recusal. I note for transparency that my research field (lipid self-assembly, membranes, amyloid) is scientifically adjacent to B063 and B062, which gives me expertise but may also bias me towards a physical-chemistry framing, and that I am a Lund University colleague of Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, which is an institutional tie to colleagues and not to any candidate.
